name: A linear interpolator in C++
brief:
Write `double interp(std::vector<double> xs, std::vector<double> ys, double x)`. It returns the straight-line value at `x` between the two nearest known points. The points may arrive unsorted, and repeated `x` values are averaged.

Below the smallest `x` or above the largest, return the nearest end value. This is a depth option for firms that ask for C++ in a research round.
constraints: Find the bracketing pair with `std::upper_bound`, not a scan.
There is at least one point, and `xs` and `ys` have the same length.
hint: Sort the pairs, merge equal x by their mean, then `std::upper_bound` gives the first x above the query. Use the pair just before it as the left end.

examples.name: Two points
examples.why: A quarter of the way from 100 to 200 is 125.
examples.note: A quarter of the way across, so a quarter of the rise of 100.

examples.name: Unsorted input
examples.why: Sort by x before you look for the bracket.

tests.name: Two points
tests.why: A quarter of the way from 100 to 200 is 125.

tests.name: Unsorted input
tests.why: Sort by x before you look for the bracket.

tests.name: Below the smallest x
tests.why: Hold the first value; do not extrapolate.

tests.name: Above the largest x
tests.why: Hold the last value; do not extrapolate.

tests.name: Repeated x, at the repeat
tests.why: The two readings at x = 1 average to 15.

tests.name: Repeated x, between
tests.why: Average the repeats first, then go halfway to 30.

tests.name: One point
tests.why: One point is both ends, so its value holds everywhere.

how: Submit runs 9 hidden tests. Each answer is accepted when it is within relative 1e-9 of the expected value.
